meeting_header: Date: 2026-06-30T15:00Z | Duration: 47m | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (Redwood SRE); Alicia Gomez, Ben Cho, Mei Lin (TideWave)
topics: eviction policies and soft vs hard eviction
prewarmed pool sizing and warmup SLAs

transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, with Priya and Ethan. quick roll call?
[00:06] Alicia: Alicia here, head of ML platform at TideWave. Ben and Mei on.
[00:10] Ben: hey all, Ben, infra.
[00:12] Mei: Mei, SRE.
[00:16] Jordan: great. today's deep dive is around how we plan capacity for bursts, priority fairness, eviction and prewarm SLAs — especially for your multi-tenant traffic. we'll walk through policy options, tradeoffs, and a sim we can run.
[00:29] Priya: quick note, i'll share the capacity-playbook PDF and a small spreadsheet after the call, links in the notes.
[00:35] Alicia: perfect. our big ask: keep interactive features p99 under 250ms during peak, while supporting native batch jobs that can be lower priority.
[00:44] Jordan: got it. can you describe peak qps and percentiles?
[00:49] Alicia: typically baseline is 400 qps, spikes up to 2.4k for 10–15 minutes a few times per day. about 35% of traffic is latency-sensitive interactive.
[01:02] Priya: okay that's helpful. so two axes: latency-sensitive customers (small tokens, short seq) and batch-heavy long seq. we'll talk about queues and priority.
[01:13] Ben: also we run in our VPC, private deployment, so prewarm semantics are tricky because we don't allow outbound control plane calls for prefetching sometimes.
[01:23] Ethan: yep we have strict egress rules, that matters for KV warmup.
[01:28] Priya: right — in Private / VPC setups we rely on local orchestrator actions vs remote control. we covered this in the last runbook but, uh, will reiterate here.
[01:37] Jordan: first, fairness model options: naive FIFO, strict priority, and weighted fair queueing (WFQ).
[01:44] Priya: FIFO is simplest but starvation happens. strict priority ensures interactive tasks win but batch jobs can be indefinitely delayed. WFQ gives weighted shares, so interactive gets a larger weight but batch gets a guaranteed min.
[01:56] Alicia: how do weights translate to real capacity numbers?
[02:00] Priya: we convert weight into token rate — e.g., interactive weight 0.7 means 70% of available execution slots under congestion. the scheduler enforces by shaping tokens per second.
[02:12] Ben: what's 'available execution slots' when we have reserved GPUs + burst pool?
[02:18] Priya: good question. we model a two-tier pool: reserved (pre-allocated GPUs) + burst (ephemeral preemptible or shared). reserved counts serve guaranteed throughput; burst absorbs extra demand. the scheduler does admission across both pools with preference rules.
[02:31] Jordan: important to talk about headroom: reserved pool should be sized to handle steady-state plus a small buffer. for example, if baseline 400 qps requires 8 GPUs at 50% util, and targets 99th latencies, you might reserve 10 GPUs, leaving headroom for short bursts while burst pool handles the remainder.
[02:51] Priya: we usually recommend sizing reserved so that steady-state plus 1–2 minute sustained increases don't need immediate burst. burst is for 5–20 minute spikes.
[03:03] Mei: warmup concerns — when a new replica starts, model KV cache is empty and the first requests see 2–3x token-latency. how do you mitigate that?
[03:13] Priya: couple of approaches: prefix/KV prefetch, background warmup traffic, and sticky session routing. prefix prefetch uses a small set of representative prompts per model to populate KV caches before marking the replica healthy. background warming is cheaper if you can run it in VPC; otherwise use short synthetic warmers.
[03:31] Ben: we can't accept external prefetch from Redwynn control plane, so we need an agent or a local warmup scheduler.
[03:37] Priya: yep in Private we provide a lightweight agent that runs warmup jobs locally. it respects egress rules and can pull warmup bundles from an on-prem artifact store.
[03:46] Alicia: how long does warmup usually take?
[03:49] Priya: depends on model size and typical prefix length. empirically between 20–90s to reach steady KV hit rates for warm networks. for longer-context services it can be 2–3 minutes.
[03:58] Jordan: that maps to warmup SLA — you can set a prewarm SLA: "replica ready for interactive traffic in < 60s". if VPC constraints, SLA might be higher.
[04:08] Ben: what about prewarmed pool sizing? we can't keep too many prewarmed replicas due to cost.
[04:12] Priya: tradeoff is cost vs tail latency. we compute expected arrivals using an M/M/c queue approximation with added warmup delay. Little's law helps: average number in system = lambda * W. we simulate using your trace to pick minimal prewarm count that keeps p99 latency under target.
[04:30] Alicia: can you run that sim?
[04:32] Jordan: yes, that's one of the next steps — Priya will run a sim with your week trace.
[04:35] Priya: we'll vary prewarm pool size, reserved counts, and burst capacity. we'll also test different eviction policies.
[04:42] Ben: eviction — we worry about noisy tenants taking down KV warm caches for interactive customers. what's safe policy?
[04:50] Priya: eviction hierarchy: soft eviction and hard eviction. soft eviction reduces concurrency for low-priority tasks first (gradual backpressure), hard eviction forcibly kills oldest or least valuable replicas when memory pressure is acute. but we also have protected caches: pinned prefixes for high-priority tenants that are excluded from eviction until a threshold.
[05:08] Mei: pinned prefixes sound useful but memory can still be exhausted. what's the policy for pinned vs non-pinned?
[05:13] Priya: pinned gets a guaranteed slice of KV budget. beyond that, eviction uses LFU with recency decay for non-pinned. we avoid pure LRU because some prefixes are hot intermittently and LRU evicts too aggressively.
[05:24] Jordan: plus we can do probabilistic prefetch for near-hot prefixes — e.g., sample requests, maintain top-100 prefixes, prefetch on scale-up.
[05:34] Alicia: batching concerns — we need low batching latency for interactive requests, but batching improves throughput and cost. what's the usual batching window?
[05:41] Priya: typical dynamic batching window is 8–20ms for interactive flows. we use adaptive windows: if queue length increases, we widen window slightly to form larger batches. for batch jobs, we allow larger windows (50–200ms).
[05:55] Ben: does dynamic batching interfere with SLOs?
[05:58] Priya: we tie batching policy to priority; high-priority requests have a max window (e.g., 15ms) and a min batch size of 1. lower-priority can wait longer to increase throughput.
[06:09] Mei: quantization fallbacks — we considered using int8 for some workloads. how do you manage quality regressions?
[06:16] Jordan: Redwood Optimize recommends candidate quant profiles per workload. approach: validate on your eval set, roll out as canary for a fraction of traffic, monitor hallucination/regression metrics, then expand. also automatic fallback to FP16 model when quality drops beyond threshold.
[06:30] Priya: in practice, quantized variants often cut token costs by 30–50% and reduce inference latency by 10–30% depending on kernels. but yes you need eval gating.
[06:40] Alicia: in bursts, would you route to quantized models first to preserve capacity?
[06:44] Priya: you can define a policy: during sustained overload, prefer quantized fallback for non-critical tenants or even for interactive with an opt-in degradation ledger. we recommend preserving a small pool of FP16 for the top-tier customers.
[06:58] Ben: how about model eviction when multiple model versions exist on the same GPU? do you evict based on last-used or predicted reuse?
[07:06] Priya: we use a hotset predictor that tracks recent usage frequency and recency, and we estimate reload cost (disk+warmup). eviction score = alpha*reload_cost + beta*frequency_score. items with lowest score evicted first.
[07:20] Jordan: that minimizes wasted cycle reloading.
[07:23] Mei: a question about burst credits and fairness — we want customers to have burst budgets so a noisy tenant can't soak everything.
[07:30] Priya: burst credits are like token buckets per account; they recharge slowly (e.g., daily). when a tenant uses burst, it consumes credits; once exhausted, they get subject to stricter WFQ weights. you can also define emergency overrides for critical traffic.
[07:44] Alicia: can credits be shared across teams within our org?
[07:48] Jordan: yes, we support hierarchical quotas: account-level and project-level credits. policy enforces parent-first usage.
[07:56] Ben: measurement: we need observability hooks — per-tenant p50/p90/p99, cache-hit rates, batch sizes, queue lengths.
[08:03] Jordan: Redwood Console exposes per-route telemetry, token cost, and KV hit metrics. we'll enable tenant tagging to get you that granularity.
[08:12] Priya: also trace examples at time buckets to debug tail latencies.
[08:16] Ben: okay good. next, let's talk about prewarm health checks and readiness gating.
[08:21] Priya: we mark a replica healthy only when KV hit-rate crosses a threshold on synthetic or sampled prefixes, and when slow-start ramp reaches target throughput. otherwise it sits in warmup pool.
[08:33] Mei: how do you measure KV hit-rate quickly?
[08:36] Priya: sample first N requests or use synthetic probes of the pinned prefix set; compute hit fraction. threshold typically 70–80% for interactive readiness.
[08:46] Alicia: what about cold starts causing p99 spikes during a rolling update?
[08:50] Jordan: rolling updates pair old and new replicas and only drain old once new are warm. for large fleets we do canary waves with staggered rollouts. also we simulate rolling update scenarios in the same burst sim.
[09:02] Ben: simulation specifics? which queueing model do you use?
[09:06] Priya: discrete-event sim with arrival trace replay, M/M/c approximations for initial sizing, and a warmup state machine per replica. we model KV warmup as a time-varying hit-rate function derived from your sample traces.
[09:20] Alicia: will the sim output per-tenant p99 and expected cost?
[09:23] Priya: yes cost estimates and per-tenant SLO breach probabilities.
[09:27] Mei: great. about eviction thresholds — what's the recommended memory margin?
[09:31] Priya: reserve 15–20% memory as scratch for transient spikes; start soft eviction at 80% and hard evict at 92–95%. thresholds depend on model memory variability.
[09:43] Ben: what about partial eviction (evict some prefixes) vs whole-model eviction?
[09:47] Priya: partial eviction is preferred: evict cold prefixes to free KV slots. whole-model eviction is last resort because reload cost and warmup penalty are high.
[09:58] Alicia: any heuristics for which prefixes to prefetch?
[10:02] Priya: we use a mix: top-k by historical frequency, recent trending prefixes, and customer-supplied 'must-warm' prefixes (for known critical flows).
[10:12] Ben: consider that some flows are long-tail but critical for certain users. can we pin those?
[10:16] Priya: yes pinned prefixes per-tenant is the mechanism. pins can be ephemeral too — you can pin for a rollout window.
[10:24] Mei: latency budget math — can you show a quick calc?
[10:28] Jordan: sure. target p99 = 250ms. baseline model single-token latency = 30ms with KV hits, KV miss penalty = +180ms. aim to keep KV miss rate under 3% for interactive. so expected p99 ~ base + miss_penalty*miss_rate. if miss_rate spikes to 10% p99 goes over SLO. hence importance of warmup and pinned prefixes.
[10:48] Priya: batching adds variable delay: if window=15ms and processing latency 30ms, overall added latency ~45ms plus any queuing. we include this in the sim.
[10:56] Ben: about reserved GPU counts: if we reserve too many we waste money; too few and we hit p99. what's the recommendation?
[11:03] Priya: run the sim to find the knee of cost vs sla breach. empirically pick the smallest reserved count that keeps baseline steady-state under target for 95% of hours, then use burst for the remaining tail.
[11:16] Alicia: in procurement we'll need clear numbers — e.g., reserve 12 GPUs, burst pool 8 across region.
[11:22] Jordan: we'll give you a few candidate mixes and cost projection.
[11:25] Mei: question: if preemptible burst instances are reclaimed, what's the fallback?
[11:31] Priya: automatic fallbacks: route to quantized variants, spill to regional hosted capacity (if allowed), or temporarily degrade non-critical responses. we ensure top-tier tenants have protected FP16 pools.
[11:44] Ben: for on-prem, can we set the system to never evict models for certain nodes?
[11:49] Priya: yes you can mark nodes as "no-evict" for reserved on-prem devices; but that reduces flexibility. it's an explicit knob.
[11:58] Alicia: security/compliance question — will prewarm artifacts or prefix lists include any sensitive customer data?
[12:05] Priya: prewarm bundles should never contain real PII; they can include synthetic prefixes or hashed tokens. for sensitive customers we use synthetic or customer-provided sanitized sets.
[12:16] Jordan: ok, quick recap so far: priority scheduling via WFQ, burst credits per org, prewarm pool with pinned prefixes, LFU-ish eviction with recency decay, partial eviction preferred, warmup SLA target around 60s for hosted but longer for private if no egress. Priya will run sims.
[12:36] Priya: also note warmup parallelism — we can parallelize prefetch across shards to reduce wall-clock warm time.
[12:43] Ben: what instrumentation will sim produce?
[12:45] Priya: per-tenant p50/p90/p99, KV hit curves, batch size distributions, cost estimates, and suggested reserve counts.
[12:55] Alicia: about rollouts and canaries — we want minimal disruption during model updates.
[12:59] Jordan: we do staged canaries and warm new variants alongside old, plus automatic rollback on quality/regression alerts.
[13:09] Mei: can regressions automatically trigger rollbacks if p99 exceeds threshold?
[13:12] Priya: yes we can set automated rollback rules.
[13:15] Ben: more about queue discipline: any work on weighted fair queuing at the kernel level vs application level?
[13:22] Priya: Redwood implements it at the scheduler layer in the runtime, close to the request admission point, not the kernel. that gives us more visibility to token costs and per-request token accounting.
[13:34] Jordan: another nuance: model-level batching vs request-level batching. for multi-tenant GPUs we prefer per-model queues to avoid cross-tenant interference.
[13:43] Alicia: okay. do you have an example of thresholds for soft vs hard eviction we can adopt?
[13:48] Priya: recommended starting point: soft start at 75% mem, aggressive soft at 82%, hard eviction at 92%. adjust by model size.
[13:57] Ben: how do we test eviction safely?
[14:00] Priya: simulate memory pressure in a staging cluster and measure SLOs when eviction runs. we also have a 'dry-run' mode to report which prefixes would evict.
[14:09] Mei: that helps. any notes on KV cache compression or quantized KV to save memory?
[14:16] Priya: some customers use compressed KV structures or lower precision for stored keys/values; it's tricky but possible. compression adds CPU overhead. Quantized KV can reduce size but increases lookup cost slightly. tradeoffs included in the sim.
[14:31] Jordan: let's talk about billing implications of reserved vs burst: reserved charged flat monthly; burst charged per-use. we can map to your finance wants.
[14:39] Alicia: yes, finance prefers predictable reserved cost for baseline.
[14:43] Priya: our recommendations will include a blended unit cost estimate for each candidate mix.
[14:49] Ben: one more VPC detail: in private, can we run warmers that live only on the cluster and are scheduled with lower priority so they don't impact live traffic?
[14:58] Priya: yes run warmers as low-priority background pods using local admission controls. they should have CPU/GPU affinity low and stop when queueing increases.
[15:07] Alicia: about monitoring — can we get alerts when warmup is slow on new replicas?
[15:12] Jordan: yes prewarm health alerts and rolling update health dashboards exist.
[15:16] Ben: any quick notes about model quant fallback latencies?
[15:20] Priya: generally quantized variants return 10–30% faster per-token; fallback switch is immediate at routing time but quality checks run in the background.
[15:30] Mei: ok, let's surface a sample timeline: we need trial sim results by next week and then a pilot with 4 reserved GPUs and a 6-GPU burst pool for two weeks.
[15:40] Jordan: noted. we'll produce the sim and suggested pilot config.
[15:44] Priya: action items as listed. we'll also include a sample watchlist for warmup metrics and recommended alert thresholds.
[15:52] Alicia: size of prewarmed pool suggestions? any quick numbers now?
[15:56] Priya: off the cuff, for your numbers maybe 2–4 prewarmed replicas per active model for interactive endpoints plus 8 reserved GPUs overall but we'll confirm with sim.
[16:07] Ben: if we do prewarmed replicas, do they increase billing as reserved?
[16:11] Jordan: depends — if prewarms are within reserved capacity no extra charge; if they're in burst instances you pay burst rates. we can design the pilot to use reserved for prewarms to reduce cost.
[16:22] Mei: any failure modes we should watch for post deploy?
[16:25] Priya: warmup runaway (warmers saturating CPU), eviction oscillation when thresholds too tight, and incorrect weight configs causing starvation. watch the console for those signals.
[16:37] Alicia: let's wrap — can you send the security docs link?
[16:40] Jordan: yes, will send SOC2 and network diagrams. link: https://redwood.app/security/tidewave-pack.pdf
[16:47] Ben: thanks. one last question — can we get a breakdown of how much slower cold KV miss is for our specific models?
[16:53] Priya: please share a sample model and token profile and we'll include concrete numbers in the sim output.
[17:00] Mei: ok sending after this call.
[17:03] Jordan: great. recap: Priya run sims, Alicia share trace and SLOs, Ethan/Ben share VPC constraints, Jordan send pricing and security docs. any other items?
[17:14] Alicia: nope that's it. thanks everyone.
[17:17] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up via email with artifacts.
[17:22] [meeting ends]
